name: Swiss Rose
lede: Swiss Rose is a dusty rose-red recorded by Maerz and Paul in 1930 at a plate position that had carried a different name, Monsoreau, in their 1892 listing of the same catalogue.

sections.title: A dustier name for an older entry
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 *A Dictionary of Color* records Swiss Rose at plate 4, position K 2, dated 1927, and the ISCC-NBS system later filed it as a moderate red [1]. The same plate position had carried the name Monsoreau in the dictionary's own 1892-dated listing, so the same catalogue slot was renamed before it reached Swiss Rose, a detail our library preserves but does not further explain [1]. The "Swiss" in the final name is, by our classification, a place-or-institution word with no documented reasoning beyond the adjective itself [2].

The nearest named colors are [[brick-rose]] and [[brick-rose]], each about 4.5 units away and both redder and duller [3].

A little further off are [[popstar]], more vivid at 4.8 units, and [[solferino]], redder at 4.9 [3]. Fashion and textile use is the field our library assigns to this name, rather than nature or painting, which fits a dusty rose more associated with cloth than with pigment [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, a color within six units of Swiss Rose covers at least five per cent of a canvas in 22 works [4]. More than half of those matches fall in the twentieth century [4]. The earliest is a work from around the year 1000 depicting a Bodhisattva, where it covers about 16 per cent of the canvas [4]. Pierre Bonnard is the strongest match, present in three of his forty-five archived paintings, over seventy times the archive's rate, and Henri Matisse's 1923 *Odalisque with a Screen* carries it across nearly a third of the canvas [4]. It is also disproportionately linked to Kalighat painting from Bengal [4]. These remain photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment tests [4]. Where it does appear, it splits mostly between mid-tone and shadow, rarely as a highlight [4].

questions.q: What name did the same catalogue plate position carry before Swiss Rose?
True or false: Swiss Rose is most strongly linked to Pierre Bonnard's paintings.

openers: Swiss Rose sits at a catalogue plate position that was named Monsoreau 35 years earlier.

issues: Monsoreau is not a color in our own data (no slug), so it is named in prose rather than linked.
